title: The Radiators of the old quarter
premise: Cyrus Sandoval, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste three years ago, returns to the old quarter of Lagos for his estranged mother's funeral, where a stranger named Ifeoma greets the family by a name no one has used in decades — 'the Radiators,' after the radiator shop that once anchored their street. As Cyrus lingers to settle the crumbling family house, Ifeoma's presence unravels a buried secret: she is the daughter of the half-brother the family erased, and the house — and the recipes written inside its walls — was promised to her line. Forced to choose between selling the house and honoring a debt of belonging, Cyrus relearns taste through the neighborhood women who cook for him, and in the final chapter he publicly renounces his inheritance at a communal feast, giving the house to Ifeoma while keeping only the name he finally says aloud.
about_author: O. M. Oyelaran is the pen name of a former food writer from Ibadan who spent a decade reviewing restaurants before turning to fiction about the families meals leave behind. The Radiators of the Old Quarter is their second novel, written in kitchens across Lagos and London.

chapters.title: The Man Who Ate Descriptions
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. In London, Cyrus writes a glowing review of a meal he cannot taste, hiding behind borrowed language. His editor praises him; Cyrus goes home to an empty flat and eats plain rice he can't feel. Emotional beat: the loneliness of professional fraud.

chapters.title: A Telephone Call About a Funeral
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. His sister Adaeze calls: their mother Funmilayo has died. Cyrus agrees to come home but negotiates a five-day stay, treating grief like a booking. Beat: avoidance dressed as practicality.

chapters.title: The Old Quarter Remembers
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Arriving in Lagos, the streets assault him with smells he can still perceive though not taste. The family house is peeling, occupied by squatters and memories. Beat: disorientation and reluctant tenderness.

chapters.title: The Stranger Who Used the Name
chapters.summary: At the wake, a young woman named Ifeoma embraces the grieving family and calls them 'the Radiators.' Silence falls. Aunt Bisi pulls Cyrus aside: nobody has said that word since 1989. Beat: the first crack in the family's arrangement.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Were
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. She explains to Cyrus the old radiator repair shop their grandfather ran, the street that gathered there, and the schism that scattered everyone — a story with a hole in the middle where a brother should be. Beat: nostalgia shadowed by deliberate omission.

chapters.title: Ifeoma Does Not Leave
chapters.summary: Ifeoma's POV. She stays past the mourning period, helping cook, learning names, quietly cataloguing the house. We learn she carries her dead father's letters and a claim she hasn't yet spoken. Beat: patient infiltration.

chapters.title: The Taste of Pepper Soup
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Mama Ngozi, the quarter's oldest cook, feeds Cyrus pepper soup on a dare. For one swallow, something flickers — heat without flavor, feeling without meaning. He weeps into the bowl. Beat: hope arriving as humiliation.

chapters.title: The Letters Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Ifeoma's POV. Repairing a floorboard, Ifeoma finds a tin: her father's letters to Funmilayo, unanswered, plus a deed fragment suggesting the house was jointly promised. Beat: proof hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Adaeze's Ledger
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Adaeze, who stayed and sacrificed, reveals she knows more than she's said — including why the brother was erased. She warns Cyrus that some inheritances are debts wearing costumes. Beat: complicity and resentment braided together.

chapters.title: The Developer's Offer
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. A property developer offers a fortune for the block, contingent on all heirs signing. The family convenes; money briefly unites what grief divided. Cyrus delays, surprising himself. Beat: temptation framed as escape.

chapters.title: Cooking Lessons
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus begins cooking with Mama Ngozi daily, tasting nothing but memorizing everything. Their lessons become confessionals; she knew his mother's secrets, including the brother, Tunde. Beat: apprenticeship as excavation.

chapters.title: Tunde, Named
chapters.summary: Ifeoma's POV. Ifeoma finally tells Cyrus plainly: Tunde was her father, disowned for marrying outside the family's approval, dying poor while the house stood on his labor. She shows the letters. Beat: the question the whole family arranged itself around, asked aloud.

chapters.title: The Family Council
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. A stormy meeting: Adaeze defends the erasure as survival; Aunt Bisi wavers; the developer's deadline looms. Ifeoma is cast out of the parlor mid-sentence. Beat: the family closing ranks around its oldest lie.

chapters.title: What Cyrus Cannot Say
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus drafts a review that will expose his lost taste and destroy his career, unable to send it. He realizes his silence about Tunde and his silence about food are the same silence. Beat: the two lies converging.

chapters.title: Mama Ngozi's Story
chapters.summary: Mama Ngozi's POV. She recounts the night Tunde was turned away from the shop door in the rain, and how Funmilayo cooked for him secretly for years — the recipes in the tin were hers. Beat: the dead mother's hidden loyalty revealed.

chapters.title: The Signature Deadline
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. With the developer's deadline days away, Adaeze prepares to sign alone, believing the sale will finally make her sacrifices worth something. Beat: desperation mistaken for resolution.

chapters.title: The Fire in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Climax part one. A kitchen fire — accidental or not — nearly destroys the house. Cyrus runs in for the tin of letters and, choking on smoke, tastes ash, then pepper soup broth someone left simmering: fully, unmistakably. Beat: taste returning through catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Feast That Was Promised
chapters.summary: Climax. At the community gathering meant to celebrate the sale, Cyrus instead reads Tunde's last letter aloud, announces his recovered tongue and his ruined credibility, and refuses to sign. He offers the house to Ifeoma. Beat: public truth-telling as climax.

chapters.title: Aftertaste
chapters.summary: Ifeoma's POV. Ifeoma, stunned, initially refuses the gift as another form of charity. Cyrus insists it isn't inheritance but repayment. She accepts on condition the kitchen stays open to the quarter. Beat: receiving without kneeling.

chapters.title: Adaeze Stays
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Stripped of the sale, Adaeze confronts her identity beyond sacrifice. Ifeoma asks her to co-run the kitchen. Adaeze says yes before she can regret it. Beat: reconciliation without absolution.

chapters.title: The Review
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus publishes his final column: a review of Mama Ngozi's pepper soup, honest about his three blind years. It ends his career and begins his life. He books no return flight. Beat: chosen exile becoming chosen home.

chapters.title: The Radiators of the Old Quarter
chapters.summary: Ensemble coda, months later. The house hums as a communal kitchen; the sign above the door is repainted with the old name. Cyrus sets tables he can finally taste from. Ifeoma lights the stove. Beat: belonging inherited at last.
